source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Address the housing issue if it interferes with medication storage, while treating transportation mainly as a scheduling inconvenience.","B":"Recognize them as social determinants that can limit access to care and influence outcomes after discharge.","C":"Classify them mainly as health-literacy problems even though the client understands the written plan.","D":"Refer them to financial counseling because their main clinical relevance is whether follow-up services can be authorized."}}
source_row.rationale: Healthy People 2030 identifies housing and transportation as social determinants of health and notes that transportation barriers can interfere with access to care and worsen outcomes. Therefore, option B best explains why the barriers belong in discharge planning even when the client understands the instructions. Option A incorrectly waits for a direct complication and minimizes transportation as merely scheduling. Option C misclassifies access barriers as health-literacy problems despite the client understanding the plan. Option D confuses social determinants with utilization management and payer authorization.

source_row.stem: A client is medically stable for discharge and understands the medication plan but has unstable housing and unreliable transportation to follow-up visits. Which interpretation best explains why these barriers remain clinically relevant?
